chunks: UART: synchronous or asynchronous. The question: Is it synchronous or asynchronous?
UART is asynchronous. That means there is no clock wire between the two devices. Each chip runs its own clock, and they only agree in advance on a speed.
Every byte is wrapped in a start bit and a stop bit, so the receiver can lock on to the timing again at the start of each byte.
Imagine two people with separate watches, set to count at the same speed. No two watches run exactly alike, so over an hour they drift apart.
But if you reset your timing at every whistle and only need to stay in step for about ten counts, the small drift never matters. The start bit is the whistle.
The watches only have to agree well enough for one frame.
The synchronous signal needs two wires (clock plus data) and the receiver just samples on the rising clock edge in the middle of each bit.
The asynchronous signal is a single wire; the receiver must make up its own sample times. The UART trace shows the alternating 'U' (0x55) pattern.
Asynchronous: no clock wire is shared. Timing comes from an agreed speed and the start bit.
Synchronous: a clock wire travels with the data, and the receiver reads data when the clock ticks. SPI is an example.
Baud rate: the agreed bits-per-second speed both ends count to.
Re-synchronization: the receiver restarts its timing at each start bit, so timing errors never build up past one frame.
Clock mismatch: how much faster or slower one chip's clock runs than the other's, as a percentage.
Two chips agree on 115200 baud, so each bit lasts about 8. 68 microseconds. The receiver reads the stop bit 9. 5 bit times after the start edge. Suppose its clock is 3% slow.
By then its reading point has drifted 9. 5 times 0. 03 equals 0. 285 of a bit. That is still inside the half-bit window, so the data is read correctly. At about 5.
3% the drift reaches half a bit, and the last bit is misread. In practice, designers budget only 3 to 4%. That is the whole idea.
"Asynchronous. There's no clock wire. Both sides pick the same baud rate and each uses its own oscillator.
To make that work, each byte is framed by a start bit and a stop bit, so the receiver can lock onto the falling start edge and then sample each bit in the middle using its own clock.
Compare that with SPI or I2C, where the clock is on a wire and the receiver samples on its edges.
Async saves a wire and tolerates unrelated clocks but costs about 20% overhead and needs the rates to match within a few percent."
